newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin against quick Chechen pullout, backs peace.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin against quick Chechen pullout, backs peace.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin gave partial backing on Thursday to a Chechnya peace plan agreed by his security tsar Alexander Lebed and the separatist rebels whom Russian forces have been trying to crush for 21 months.
He qualified his acceptance by saying Russia should not rush into withdrawing its troops.

"I have backed the latest plan of action with the exception of one issue -- the fast and prompt withdrawal of troops -- I think we should not be in a hurry to do that," Yeltsin said in a television interview.

But Lebed was quoted by Itar-Tass news agency as saying after talks with Chechen chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov that the pullout would start on Sunday, September 8. It seemed likely he was not aware of Yeltsin's comments.
Lebed's peace plan includes a compromise on the central issue -- independence for the mainly Moslem North Caucasus region -- by agreeing to put off a decision for five years.
The accord, signed by Lebed and Maskhadov last Saturday, foresees the withdrawal of most of the troops with Russian-rebel joint patrols taking their place in the capital Grozny.

Yeltsin did not make clear how long he wanted his forces to stay in the region, but the rebels have always said a complete troop withdrawal was a condition for peace and they were likely to react angrily to his announcement.
Yeltsin, 65, who emerged from weeks of seclusion to say he would to have heart surgery this month, was giving his first public reaction to Lebed's deal, which many have seen as a climbdown by Moscow.
Lebed and Maskhadov earlier met in the village of Novye Atagi, 25 km (15 miles) south of Grozny, to agree measures to build on the truce and a political deal aimed at ending the conflict.

Lebed said afterwards that more joint patrols would be sent in and new provisional bodies set up to maintain order. "We have agreed to increase the number of members of joint units," he told reporters.

"We agreed to set up joint law enforcement bodies because it is not enough to catch criminals. They should be put in prison, we need a prosecutor to deal with them and we need judges who will try them."
Lebed said he and Maskhadov had agreed to make Grozny a demilitarised zone in which only members of the joint patrols would be allowed to carry guns.
"We have agreed to continue the peace process which is going ahead with difficulty and which has opponents on both sides and among criminal, bandit structures," he said.

Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying before the talks that he was worried by reports of separatists seizing hostages and persecuting supporters of pro-Moscow authorities in the breakaway region. Rebel leaders have denied the reports.

"Each time Alexander Ivanovich (Lebed) comes here full of negative and untrue information," Maskhadov told reporters afterwards. "Now we have convinced him that we are not going to persecute, jail, rob or kill anyone."

The rebels, who celebrate the fifth anniversary of their unilateral declaration of independence on Friday, view Chechnya as a separate state. Moscow says the region must stay part of the Russian Federation.
